name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Sequence of events during bimolecular nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text:
Consider the following events occurring during the bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) reaction between chloromethane and hydroxide ion:

(I) Backside approach of the incoming hydroxide nucleophile toward the partially positive carbon atom directly opposite to the departing chlorine atom.
(II) Formation of a pentacoordinate transition state in which all three carbon–hydrogen bonds become coplanar while carbon is simultaneously partially bonded to both incoming and outgoing groups.
(III) Cleavage of the carbon–chlorine bond with departure of the chloride ion as the leaving group, accompanied by inversion of spatial configuration.
(IV) Formation of the final methanol product displaying complete stereochemical inversion.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of these stages?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Reaction Overview
The process under evaluation is the concerted \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) displacement reaction between chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\)) and hydroxide ion (\(\mathrm{OH^-}\)) to produce methanol (\(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\)) and chloride ion (\(\mathrm{Cl^-}\)).

Step 2: Fundamental Principles of the Bimolecular Mechanism
The \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction proceeds as a concerted, single-step mechanism without any stable intermediate. The incoming electron-rich nucleophile must approach the electrophilic carbon from the direction opposite to the carbon–halogen bond to minimize electrostatic repulsion and allow productive orbital overlap.

Step 3: Logical Order of Mechanistic Events
1. The process begins when the incoming nucleophile approaches the substrate from the backside (opposite the leaving chlorine atom).
2. As the incoming nucleophile approaches and begins forming a bond, the three non-reacting carbon–hydrogen bonds flatten into a single plane, producing an unstable transition state where the central carbon is simultaneously partially bonded to five groups.
3. The carbon–halogen bond weakens further until the chloride ion fully departs as a leaving group, accompanied by the flipping of the three remaining bonds in the manner of an umbrella turning inside out (Walden inversion).
4. The departure completes the formation of the inverted substitution product, methanol.

Step 4: Verification of Sequence
The chronological order proceeds strictly as: backside approach of the nucleophile \(\rightarrow\) transition state assembly \(\rightarrow\) departure of chloride with configurational inversion \(\rightarrow\) formation of the final inverted alcohol molecule. This matches the progression (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct sequential order is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Sequence of steps in Grignard hydrocarbon synthesis

questiontext.text:
Consider the conversion of bromoethane into ethane using magnesium metal followed by reaction with water:

(I) Reaction of bromoethane with magnesium metal suspended in dry diethyl ether.
(II) Insertion of magnesium to yield ethylmagnesium bromide possessing a highly polarized carbon–magnesium bond.
(III) Protonation of the strongly basic carbanionic ethyl group through reaction with water.
(IV) Formation of ethane hydrocarbon along with basic magnesium halide, \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)Br}\).

Arrange these stages in the correct chronological sequence.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Transformations
The pathway outlines the synthesis of an organomagnesium reagent (Grignard reagent) from an alkyl halide and its subsequent protonolysis to generate a hydrocarbon.

Step 2: Governing Chemical Principles
Grignard reagents are synthesized by reacting haloalkanes with magnesium turnings in anhydrous ether. The carbon–magnesium bond is highly polarized with partial negative charge on carbon (\(\mathrm{R^{\delta-}-Mg^{\delta+}X}\)). Because of this pronounced carbanionic character, it reacts readily with any source of acidic protons (such as water) to yield the corresponding alkane.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Reaction Sequence
1. Initially, bromoethane is brought into contact with magnesium in dry ether.
2. Magnesium reacts to form ethylmagnesium bromide (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2MgBr}\)).
3. Subsequently, treatment with water causes the ethyl group to abstract a proton from the \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) molecule.
4. Finally, the proton transfer yields the alkane (ethane, \(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\)) and the inorganic byproduct \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)Br}\).

Step 4: Check of Continuity
Reagent formation must precede proton transfer because the carbanion does not exist prior to carbon–magnesium bond formation, and the hydrocarbon product is isolated only following protonolysis. Hence, the logical order is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological sequence is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Sequential stages in unimolecular nucleophilic substitution mechanism

questiontext.text:
Consider the hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide) to tert-butyl alcohol under polar protic conditions via the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism:

(I) Solvation of the leaving halide group by the polar protic solvent, assisting the reversible heterolysis of the carbon–bromine bond.
(II) Slow cleavage of the polarized \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond yielding a planar, \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbocation intermediate and a bromide ion.
(III) Rapid nucleophilic attack of the nucleophile on either face of the planar, achiral carbocation intermediate.
(IV) Completion of bond formation yielding 2-methylpropan-2-ol as the substitution product.

What is the correct logical sequence of these mechanistic stages?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reaction and Mechanism
The reaction is the conversion of \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CBr}\) to \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH}\) following unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)).

Step 2: Principles of \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) Kinetics and Mechanism
The \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism is a two-step process occurring through an ionic intermediate. Step I involves slow heterolytic cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond facilitated by solvent solvation energy. Step II involves fast combination of the carbocation with the nucleophile.

Step 3: Sequential Breakdown
1. In polar protic solvents, hydrogen bonding and ion-dipole solvation of the departing bromide ion help weaken and polarize the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond.
2. Heterolysis of the polarized bond takes place in the rate-determining step to generate a planar, trigonal \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbocation intermediate and free bromide ion.
3. Once the planar intermediate forms, the nucleophile attacks rapidly from either the top or bottom lobe of the unhybridized \(p\)-orbital.
4. The covalent bond forms, giving the final alcohol product.

Step 4: Consistency Check
A carbocation cannot be attacked before it is formed, and the slow heterolytic cleavage relies on solvent assistance. Therefore, the ordered pathway is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct logical sequence is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Sequence of reactions in Sandmeyer chlorobenzene synthesis

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following experimental and chemical stages in the synthesis of chlorobenzene starting from aniline via Sandmeyer's reaction in their correct chronological sequence:

(I) Dissolution or suspension of primary aromatic amine (aniline) in cold aqueous mineral acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)).
(II) Treatment of the cold acidic amine solution with aqueous sodium nitrite (\(\mathrm{NaNO}_2\)) at 273–278 K.
(III) Formation of a freshly prepared solution containing benzenediazonium chloride.
(IV) Mixing the freshly prepared diazonium salt solution with cuprous chloride (\(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}\)) to replace the diazonium group and evolve nitrogen gas.

The correct sequential order of these stages is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Synthesis
The task requires ordering the stages of the Sandmeyer reaction starting from aniline to yield chlorobenzene.

Step 2: Principles of Diazotization and Cuprous Halide Displacement
Primary aromatic amines react with nitrous acid (\(\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HX}\)) at low temperature (273–278 K) to form stable diazonium salts. Because diazonium salts decompose at elevated temperatures, they are prepared in situ and immediately mixed with cuprous chloride to displace the \(\mathrm{-N_2^+}\) group with \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), liberating \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Chemical Progression
1. Aniline is first dissolved or suspended in cold aqueous hydrochloric acid.
2. Sodium nitrite solution is added under ice cooling (273–278 K) to generate nitrous acid in situ.
3. Diazotization occurs to yield a solution of benzenediazonium chloride (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-}\)).
4. The diazonium salt solution is combined with cuprous chloride (\(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}\)), causing dinitrogen evolution and delivering chlorobenzene.

Step 4: Check of Continuity
The diazotization reaction requires an acidic medium before nitrite addition, and cuprous chloride can only act on the pre-formed diazonium salt. Thus, the order is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct sequential order of stages is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Sequential stages in nucleophilic aromatic substitution mechanism

questiontext.text:
In the conversion of 4-chloronitrobenzene into 4-nitrophenol by treatment with warm aqueous sodium hydroxide followed by acidification, arrange the following mechanistic stages in their correct logical sequence:

(I) Nucleophilic addition of hydroxide ion to the \(sp^2\) aromatic carbon bearing the chlorine atom.
(II) Formation of a resonance-stabilized carbanionic Meisenheimer intermediate with negative charge delocalized onto the ortho and para positions and into the nitro group.
(III) Rapid expulsion of chloride ion as a leaving group, re-establishing the aromatic sextet.
(IV) Protonation of the phenoxide species upon acidification to produce 4-nitrophenol.

The correct sequential order of these stages is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Reaction and Conditions
The reaction is the nucleophilic aromatic substitution (addition-elimination, \(\mathrm{S_NAr}\)) of 4-chloronitrobenzene with aqueous sodium hydroxide at 443 K followed by acidification.

Step 2: Mechanism of Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution
Aryl halides are generally unreactive toward nucleophilic attack due to resonance stabilization and partial double-bond character of the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond. However, strong electron-withdrawing groups (such as \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\)) at ortho or para positions stabilize the negative charge developed in the transition state and intermediate through resonance.

Step 3: Detailed Sequence of Events
1. The hydroxide ion attacks the ring carbon bearing the halogen atom in a slow, rate-determining addition step.
2. A resonance-stabilised carbanion intermediate forms where negative charge is accommodated by the ring carbons and directly delocalized into the oxygen atoms of the para-nitro group.
3. In a subsequent fast elimination step, the chloride ion departs, restoring aromaticity to give 4-nitrophenoxide.
4. Acidification (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) protonates the phenoxide oxygen to yield neutral 4-nitrophenol.

Step 4: Check of Continuity
Elimination of chloride cannot occur before the carbanion is created by nucleophilic addition, and acidification is the final workup step. Thus, the order is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct sequential order is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Chronological stages of atmospheric ozone depletion by freons

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following sequential atmospheric and chemical processes associated with the release and action of Freon-12 (\(\mathrm{CCl_2F_2}\)) in the correct chronological progression:

(I) Release of volatile Freon-12 into the troposphere from aerosol propellants and refrigeration equipment.
(II) Upward diffusion of unreactive, stable Freon-12 molecules unchanged into the stratosphere.
(III) Photochemical homolysis of carbon–chlorine bonds by intense stratospheric ultraviolet radiation, generating chlorine free radicals.
(IV) Catalytic breakdown of stratospheric ozone into molecular oxygen via chlorine radical chain reactions, disrupting the ozone layer.

Which sequence correctly reflects these sequential environmental events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Environmental Chemistry Principles
Freons (chlorofluorocarbons) are exceptionally stable and non-reactive in the lower atmosphere (troposphere). Due to their chemical inertness, they do not undergo degradation near the Earth's surface.

Step 2: Atmospheric Transport and Stratospheric Photochemistry
Because of their persistence, chlorofluorocarbons slowly diffuse upward across the troposphere into the stratosphere over prolonged periods. Once in the stratosphere, high-energy solar ultraviolet radiation dissociates the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond to produce chlorine free radicals (\(\mathrm{Cl^\bullet}\)).

Step 3: Radical Chain Depletion
The liberated chlorine free radicals participate in catalytic chain cycles with ozone molecules (\(\mathrm{O_3}\)), converting them to dioxygen (\(\mathrm{O_2}\)) and regenerating chlorine radicals to continue the destructive cycle.

Step 4: Chronological Ordering
The chain of events follows sequentially: release at ground level \(\rightarrow\) diffusion into the stratosphere \(\rightarrow\) photochemical production of chlorine radicals \(\rightarrow\) catalytic breakdown of ozone. This corresponds to (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct sequence of events is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Chronological order of historical discoveries in stereochemistry

questiontext.text:
The textbook highlights several foundational historical milestones in the development of organic stereochemistry and organohalogen chemistry:

(I) Louis Pasteur's discovery that crystals of certain compounds exist as non-superimposable mirror images showing opposite optical rotation.
(II) J. Van't Hoff and C. Le Bel's proposal of tetrahedral geometry and asymmetric carbon atoms as the origin of molecular chirality.
(III) Alexander Zaitsev's formulation of the empirical rule governing the regioselectivity of alkene formation in dehydrohalogenation.
(IV) Victor Grignard's discovery of organomagnesium halides (Grignard reagents).
(V) Paul Muller's discovery of the effectiveness of \(\mathrm{p,p^\prime}\)-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) as an insecticide.

Arrange these historical milestones in chronological order from earliest to latest.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Listing Historical Events with Stated Dates
According to the historical accounts documented in the chapter:
- Louis Pasteur observed enantiomeric crystal morphology and optical rotation in 1848.
- J. Van't Hoff and C. Le Bel independently proposed the tetrahedral carbon model and asymmetric stereocentres in 1874.
- Alexander Zaitsev formulated the rule of preferential formation of the more substituted alkene during \(\beta\)-elimination in 1875.
- Victor Grignard reported the preparation of alkylmagnesium halides in dry ether in 1900.
- Paul Muller discovered the insecticidal properties of DDT in 1939.

Step 2: Comparison of Dates
Arranging the years chronologically:
1848 \(\rightarrow\) 1874 \(\rightarrow\) 1875 \(\rightarrow\) 1900 \(\rightarrow\) 1939.

Step 3: Matching Events with Chronology
- Earliest (1848): Pasteur's optical rotation of enantiomorphic crystals.
- Second (1874): Van't Hoff and Le Bel's tetrahedral carbon concept.
- Third (1875): Zaitsev's dehydrohalogenation rule.
- Fourth (1900): Grignard's discovery of organomagnesium reagents.
- Latest (1939): Muller's discovery of the insecticidal utility of DDT.

Step 4: Check of Continuity
The chronological sequence is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV) \(\rightarrow\) (V).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct chronological order is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV) \(\rightarrow\) (V).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_SEQUENCING_Q08 - Sequence of steps in conversion of isomeric bromopropanes

questiontext.text:
To convert secondary alkyl halide 2-bromopropane into its primary structural isomer 1-bromopropane, arrange the following experimental and chemical stages in their correct logical sequence:

(I) Heating 2-bromopropane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{alc.\ KOH}\)) to carry out dehydrohalogenation.
(II) Isolation of the formed propene alkene gas.
(III) Addition of gaseous hydrogen bromide (\(\mathrm{HBr}\)) to propene in the presence of an organic peroxide.
(IV) Anti-Markovnikov free radical addition yielding 1-bromopropane as the major product.

What is the correct sequential order of steps for this synthetic transformation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Synthetic Goal
The conversion requires transposing the halogen position from \(\mathrm{C-2}\) in 2-bromopropane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_3}\)) to \(\mathrm{C-1}\) in 1-bromopropane (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Br}\)).

Step 2: Chemical Principles and Pathway Design
Direct nucleophilic displacement of bromide cannot relocate the functional group to an adjacent carbon. The established two-stage pathway involves:
1. Elimination of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) using a strong base (\(\mathrm{alcoholic\ KOH}\)) to generate propene alkene.
2. Regioselective addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) across the alkene unsaturation in an anti-Markovnikov manner using organic peroxide (peroxide effect / Kharasch effect).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Sequence
1. 2-Bromopropane is heated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide, abstracting a \(\beta\)-proton and losing bromide ion (\(\beta\)-elimination).
2. Propene (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2}\)) is collected as the alkene intermediate.
3. Propene is treated with hydrogen bromide in the presence of an organic peroxide.
4. The reaction proceeds via a free-radical chain mechanism, directing the bromine radical to the terminal carbon to give 1-bromopropane as the major product.

Step 4: Check of Continuity
Alkene formation must precede the peroxide-catalyzed addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\). The logical progression is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct sequence of steps is (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).
